description: First 50 seeds only - testing 'starting well' quality

scoring_criteria.9: Perfect native speech in both languages
scoring_criteria.1-2: Marginal, no one would say this

phrases.english: Do you understand what I'm saying?
phrases.notes: Natural in both languages. Korean uses indirect question form correctly. 'understand what I'm saying' maps well to 무슨 말인지 이해하다.

phrases.english: She wants to answer carefully
phrases.notes: Good Korean structure with 싶어해요 for third person desire. 그녀는 is slightly formal/literary; Koreans often drop pronouns or use names.

phrases.english: We are learning about it
phrases.notes: Grammatically correct. 그것에 대해 is a bit formal; native speakers might just say 그거 배우고 있어요 in casual speech.

phrases.english: She started to think about learning Korean
phrases.other: 그녀는 한국어를 배우는 것에 대해 생각하기 시작했어요
phrases.notes: Grammatically correct but wordy. Korean is a bit textbook-ish with 것에 대해. More natural: 한국어 배울 생각을 하기 시작했어요.

phrases.english: He is thinking about it carefully
phrases.other: 그는 그것에 대해 신중하게 생각하고 있어요
phrases.notes: Grammatically sound. 그것에 대해 is formal but acceptable in polite speech.

phrases.english: I started learning Korean last month
phrases.notes: Natural and idiomatic in both languages. Good use of 배우기 시작하다.

phrases.english: When I am here I speak Korean
phrases.other: 저는 여기 있을 때 한국어로 말해요
phrases.notes: Both languages natural. Good conditional with 때. Correct particle 로 for 'in Korean'.

phrases.english: We started to think about it last month
phrases.other: 우리는 지난달에 그것에 대해 생각하기 시작했어요
phrases.notes: Correct structure. 그것에 대해 is slightly formal but acceptable in polite speech.

phrases.english: I want to learn Korean easily
phrases.notes: Natural in both languages. Good adverb placement with 쉽게.

phrases.english: I want to speak with you
phrases.notes: English is natural but 당신 is awkward in spoken Korean - it's either too formal or can sound confrontational depending on context. Better: 같이 얘기하고 싶어요 or use the person's name/title.

phrases.english: She is tired this afternoon
phrases.notes: Grammatically correct. 그녀는 is literary; would typically use name or drop pronoun in natural speech.

phrases.english: I want to practise speaking Korean
phrases.notes: Both natural. Good nominalization with 말하기를.

phrases.english: She wants to come back at six o'clock
phrases.notes: Good use of 싶어해요 for third person. 그녀는 is literary but acceptable. 돌아오다 is correct.

phrases.english: We are thinking about it
phrases.notes: Grammatically correct with progressive form. 그것에 대해 is formal but acceptable.

phrases.english: He is going to start soon
phrases.notes: Natural in both languages. Good future tense with -ㄹ 거예요.

phrases.english: to be useful
phrases.notes: Dictionary form appropriate for 'to be useful'. Clean and correct.

phrases.english: She wants to learn Korean soon
phrases.notes: Correct grammar with 싶어해요 for third person desire. 그녀는 is literary.

phrases.english: She is learning Korean for a month
phrases.other: 그녀는 한 달 동안 한국어를 배우고 있어요
phrases.notes: English is slightly awkward - 'has been learning for a month' would be more natural. Korean uses 동안 correctly but the present progressive may not capture the duration sense perfectly.

phrases.english: She is not going to be able to come back
phrases.notes: Both natural. Good combination of ability (수 없다) and future (-ㄹ 거예요).

phrases.english: I want to speak Korean with you
phrases.notes: 당신 is problematic - rarely used naturally in Korean. Would be better with name/title or 같이.

phrases.english: I like the feeling of being ready
phrases.notes: Slightly unusual phrasing in both languages but grammatically correct Korean.

phrases.english: I'm trying to learn how to speak often
phrases.other: 저는 자주 말하는 방법을 배우려고 해요
phrases.notes: English is awkward - 'how to speak often' doesn't quite make sense. Korean mirrors the awkwardness.

phrases.english: He wants to learn to speak Korean quickly
phrases.other: 그는 빨리 한국어로 말하는 것을 배우고 싶어해요
phrases.notes: Grammatically correct. 말하는 것을 배우다 is a bit wordy but acceptable.

phrases.english: I feel good this morning
phrases.notes: Perfect. Natural in both languages. Idiomatic Korean with 기분이 좋다.

phrases.english: We are all a little tired
phrases.notes: Excellent. Natural in both languages. Good use of 모두 and 조금.

phrases.english: Do you want to learn how to say something?
phrases.notes: Correct grammar. 뭔가 is natural colloquial form of 무언가.

phrases.english: Answering quickly is useful
phrases.notes: Good nominalization. Natural in both languages.

phrases.english: how to say something often
phrases.notes: English is awkward as a phrase fragment. 'How to say something often' is semantically odd. Korean mirrors this.

phrases.english: Do you want to speak Korean with someone else?
phrases.notes: Natural in both. Good use of 다른 사람.

phrases.english: I want to speak now
phrases.notes: Perfect. Simple, natural, and correct in both languages.

phrases.english: how to say a word in Korean
phrases.notes: Correct and natural phrase structure in both languages.

phrases.english: I'm trying to speak with you now
phrases.notes: 당신 issue again - unnatural in spoken Korean. Otherwise grammatically correct.

phrases.english: I am learning something new
phrases.notes: Excellent. Natural in both languages. Good use of progressive form.

phrases.english: We want to meet as soon as possible
phrases.other: 우리는 가능한 한 빨리 만나고 싶어요
phrases.notes: Good. 가능한 한 빨리 is the correct idiom for 'as soon as possible'.

phrases.english: He is going to learn this afternoon
phrases.notes: Natural in both. Good future tense construction.

phrases.english: He wanted to help me last month
phrases.notes: Good past tense of desire (싶었어요). 도와주다 correctly adds giving nuance.

phrases.english: Do you want to do it?
phrases.notes: Perfect. Simple, direct, natural in both languages.

phrases.english: about/approximately
phrases.notes: Correct vocabulary item. 약 is the standard term for 'approximately'.

phrases.english: She was thinking about how to answer yesterday
phrases.other: 그녀는 어제 어떻게 대답해야 할지 생각하고 있었어요
phrases.notes: Good use of 어떻게...할지 for indirect question. 그녀는 is literary but correct.

phrases.english: making mistakes
phrases.notes: Perfect nominalization. 실수하다 is the natural verb for making mistakes.

phrases.english: I have a feeling as if I am nearly ready
phrases.other: 저는 거의 준비가 된 것 같은 기분이에요
phrases.notes: English is a bit awkward ('I have a feeling as if'). Korean mirrors this with a complex construction that works but is wordy.

phrases.english: I want to speak carefully
phrases.notes: Good in both languages. 신중하게 works well for 'carefully' in speech context.

phrases.english: We think meeting this afternoon is a good thing
phrases.other: 우리는 오늘 오후에 만나는 것이 좋은 것이라고 생각해요
phrases.notes: English is awkward ('is a good thing' - would say 'is a good idea' or just 'we think we should meet'). Korean is very literal and wordy with 좋은 것이라고.

phrases.english: We don't want to be quiet
phrases.notes: Both work. 조용히 있다 for 'be quiet' is correct.

phrases.english: She says that feeling tired is a good thing sometimes
phrases.other: 그녀는 가끔 피곤한 것이 좋은 것이라고 말해요
phrases.notes: English slightly awkward ('feeling tired is a good thing'). Korean 좋은 것이라고 is wordy - more natural: 피곤한 것도 때로는 좋다고.

phrases.english: after you finish
phrases.notes: 당신이 is problematic - should drop or replace. Also 끝나면 implies 'when it ends' (intransitive) - 끝내면 would be better for 'when you finish' (transitive).

phrases.english: We want to meet at six o'clock
phrases.notes: Perfect. Simple, natural, correct time particle 에.

phrases.english: Are you going to help me easily?
phrases.notes: English is slightly awkward - 'help me easily' is an unusual collocation. Korean is grammatically fine.

phrases.english: But we don't want to stop talking
phrases.other: 하지만 우리는 말하는 것을 멈추고 싶지 않아요
phrases.notes: Good in both languages. 말하는 것을 멈추다 works well.

phrases.english: I'm going to practise speaking Korean
phrases.notes: Natural in both. Good future tense and nominalization.

phrases_below_5.reason: 당신이 is unnatural in Korean; also 끝나다 (intransitive) vs 끝내다 (transitive) issue

worst_3_phrases.reason: Two issues: (1) 당신 is rarely used naturally in Korean - sounds formal/confrontational; (2) 끝나다 is intransitive ('to end') but should be 끝내다 (transitive, 'to finish something'). Should be something like '끝나면' (without subject) or '다 하면'.

worst_3_phrases.english: I want to speak with you
worst_3_phrases.reason: 당신 is problematic in Korean - it can sound either overly formal or confrontational depending on context. Native speakers would use the person's name/title or 같이 ('together').

worst_3_phrases.english: I want to speak Korean with you
worst_3_phrases.reason: Same 당신 issue - this pronoun is rarely used naturally in spoken Korean.

common_issues.explanation: 당신 is rarely natural in Korean conversation. It can sound formal, distant, or even confrontational. Native speakers typically use names, titles, or simply drop the subject.

While grammatically correct, 그녀 especially feels more literary/written. In speech, Koreans usually use names or drop pronouns when context is clear. Not marked down heavily as it's acceptable in formal/polite speech.
Grammatically correct but more formal than casual speech. Native speakers might use 그거 or restructure the sentence.

summary.overall_assessment: Round 3 shows strong quality overall (average 7.14/9). The course demonstrates good Korean grammar including proper use of honorific levels (-요 endings), desire expressions (싶다/싶어하다), and nominalization patterns. Main recurring issue is the use of 당신 which is unnatural in spoken Korean. The 그녀/그는 pronouns are acceptable but slightly literary. Most phrases would be understood and are grammatically correct, with several achieving native-level naturalness.
